summary: Deep dive on Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture for a pilot. Discussed network isolation strategies, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS integration, audit logs, SOC 2/ISO artifacts, SSO/RBAC, and pilot next steps. Action items assigned to both Redwood and Sterling. Some transcription errors present (KV cache referenced as K-V cash, etc.).
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we really appreciate you taking the time. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Marco our SE and Sanjay from solutions.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Hi Lena, thanks. Priya here, CISO at Sterling. We've got Elena and Rafael on as well.
[00:18] Tom Blake: Hey all, Tom, head of cloud infra. Quick note we got about an hour.
[00:25] Marco Diaz: Great, agenda is basically a network + security deep dive for the private VPC deployment, cover ingress/egress, firewalling, KMS, audit/logging and any compliance artifacts.
[00:35] Elena Morris: Sounds good. Our primary concerns are network isolation, preventing exfil, and making sure audit trails meet our SOC 2 needs.
[00:44] Sanjay Rao: Perfect, we'll walk through recommended topology then dig into policies, and then we can map to your requirements.
[00:50] [01:00] Marco Diaz: Quick high level — Redwood Private runs a control plane that can be customer-managed in a VPC, and the inference runtime lives inside the customer's network. For Sterling's pilot we recommend dedicated subnets for control plane egress, inference workers, and management.
[01:18] Tom Blake: When you say control plane egress, does that require any outbound connectivity to Redwood? We want to avoid traffic to public endpoints where possible.
[01:26] Lena Park: Good question. We have two deployment modes for private: fully private with a customer-managed control plane and periodic artifacts exchange, or an option where the control plane is in our managed environment but the data plane stays in your VPC. For full isolation we can do a customer-hosted control plane — that needs no egress to Redwood.
[01:44] Priya Nair: So customer-hosted control plane means we host the control plane services in our VPC or on-prem and Redwood provides the binaries/config?
[01:52] Sanjay Rao: Yes, that's right. We provide a private control plane image + helm charts (or tarball for on-prem) and you run it. For the pilot we typically do a shared control plane in your VPC with restricted egress only to STS/KMS endpoints if needed.
[02:08] Rafael Gomez: Are those STS/KMS calls mandatory? Our KMS is on-prem HSM, we don't want keys leaving the network.
[02:16] Marco Diaz: You can absolutely bring-your-own-KMS/HSM. For on-prem HSM we integrate via standard PKCS#11 or KMIP if you prefer. We don't require keys to leave your network — the runtime can talk to your HSM over private connectivity. Sometimes we use a KMS proxy.
[02:31] Elena Morris: Ok and audit logs — how are they surfaced? We need immutable logs for all inference requests and admin operations for SOC 2 audit.
[02:40] Sanjay Rao: We emit detailed audit events to a customer-configured log sink — S3, GCS, or an on-prem syslog. Events include auth events, model loads, inference request metadata (no raw customer PII), and control plane admin actions. You can ship those to your SIEM.
[02:54] Priya Nair: You said no raw PII — we need to be sure token-level logs don't contain user content. Is there a redaction layer?
[03:02] Marco Diaz: Good point. We redact request/response full payloads by default in audit mode. We do include metadata like request size, model used, latency, and request hashes. If you need full transcripts for debugging we can enable a secure store with stricter access controls, but that's optional.
[03:18] [03:30] Tom Blake: Network specifics — we want to validate egress locking. Can you run with zero internet egress except to our internal NTP and internal registries?
[03:39] Sanjay Rao: Yes. For air-gapped environments we support local registries and no outbound egress. The only operations that usually need multicast or so are updates; you can disable automatic updates.
[03:48] Elena Morris: How do you protect against data exfil from model caches or KV cache — sometimes called KV cache — we've seen it called K-V cash in notes —
[03:58] Marco Diaz: (chuckles) transcription friendly — KV cache. The runtime keeps keys in memory and ephemeral disk. We recommend encrypting ephemeral disks with your key and ensuring that the worker nodes have no route to external storage. Also enforce strict egress firewall rules so only approved management IPs can reach control endpoints.
[04:15] Rafael Gomez: For firewalling — do you have sample iptables rules or managed security groups?
[04:21] Sanjay Rao: Yes, we can share a starter iptables ruleset and cloud security group templates. For example, block 0.0.0.0/0 egress on worker subnets and allow only specific CIDRs for your admin zone and KMS. We also recommend stateful inspection on the outbound path.
[04:36] [04:50] Priya Nair: SSO and RBAC — we need SAML 2.0 enterprise SSO and role-based access that maps to our internal IAM groups. How does Redwood integrate?
[04:58] Marco Diaz: We support SAML 2.0 and OIDC. For RBAC we integrate with your identity provider via SCIM to sync groups, or you can map roles manually. Admin roles are audit logged.
[05:10] Elena Morris: Any support for fine-grained resource scoping? e.g., team A can only deploy models to their reserved pool and can't access team B's models.
[05:17] Sanjay Rao: Yes, we have tenant scoping and per-project role permissions. You can lock model access to specific projects and use network policies to isolate the worker pools.
[05:25] [05:40] Tom Blake: Encryption at rest — you said ephemeral disk encryption. What about model artifacts stored in S3 or on shared volumes?
[05:47] Marco Diaz: All persisted artifacts can be stored encrypted using your managed KMS keys. We support CMEK in cloud or you can pre-encrypt artifacts before upload for extra assurance.
[05:57] Rafael Gomez: Data residency — we need all data to remain in our US-East region for now. Is that configurable?
[06:03] Lena Park: Absolutely. Private deployment inherits your region constraints; you control where workloads run. For hosted options we can pin to region but for private/on-prem it's fully controlled by you.
[06:12] [06:30] Priya Nair: Ok stepping through an example ingress/egress flow: client app calls our internal API, which forwards prompt to Redwood runtime in our VPC, runtime returns response. We want to ensure there is no unexpected outbound call to third parties.
[06:44] Marco Diaz: In the fully private model there are no outbound third-party calls. We recommend service endpoints be internal-only. If you enable telemetry or optional telemetry to Redwood, that's an explicit opt-in and goes over a secure, whitelisted egress.
[06:58] Tom Blake: Can you enumerate the outbound ports and destinations the runtime needs if we do opt into managed control plane?
[07:06] Sanjay Rao: Sure. For a managed control plane you typically allow egress to these endpoints (TLS 443): control plane endpoint IPs, STS endpoints for identity, KMS endpoints if you use cloud KMS, and container registry endpoints for image pulls. We will provide exact CIDR ranges for the managed control plane.
[07:22] Elena Morris: We have strict firewalling, any chance of certificate pinning or mutual TLS for control plane connections?
[07:30] Marco Diaz: Yes, we support mTLS between control plane and workers for mutual authentication and you can pin certificates. For customer-managed control planes mTLS is the recommended pattern.
[07:40] [07:55] Priya Nair: About audit windows — how long are control plane and inference logs retained by Redwood if we use managed logging?
[08:02] Lena Park: By default our hosted retention is 90 days but for enterprise we can extend or you can push logs to your retention system. For private deployments you control retention since logs go to your sinks.
[08:12] Rafael Gomez: For the pilot we want to keep logs for 1 year in our SIEM.
[08:16] Marco Diaz: That works — push to your S3/GCS or syslog with lifecycle policies.
[08:22] [08:40] Tom Blake: Remediation and incident response — if a host is compromised, what's the containment story?
[08:48] Sanjay Rao: We recommend network ACLs and ephemeral worker machines that are cycled frequently. For containment you can revoke a worker's cert, remove it from the cluster, and trigger node replacement. Audit logs show API keys and admin actions tied to identities.
[08:59] Elena Morris: How are service credentials handled? Do workers need long-lived keys?
[09:05] Marco Diaz: We use short-lived tokens for inter-service auth and recommend rotated service identities via your IAM. Long-lived keys are discouraged; we can integrate with your IAM to mint ephemeral creds.
[09:15] [09:30] Priya Nair: Encryption in transit — TLS only? Any gRPC encryption quirks?
[09:35] Sanjay Rao: All control and data plane communication is TLS 1.2+/1.3. gRPC over TLS is supported. For extra assurance we recommend mTLS and internal CA.
[09:45] Tom Blake: How about firewalling at the application layer — do you have WAF integration?
[09:50] Marco Diaz: Redwood doesn't provide a WAF out of the box for model inference, but we integrate with existing WAFs and can place inference endpoints behind your application gateway.
[09:58] [10:15] Rafael Gomez: A practical question — during model downloads or artifacts updates, are images pulled from public registries? We can't allow public pulls.
[10:23] Marco Diaz: For the private deployment we advise using your internal container registry. We can provide images for you to import into your registry. No public pulls are required.
[10:32] Elena Morris: On-prem options — for air-gapped sites, do you support a full offline install?
[10:37] Sanjay Rao: Yes, full offline install is supported. We provide installers and a runbook. The only limitation is you won't get automatic remote updates, obviously.
[10:46] [10:55] Priya Nair: One of our compliance auditors asked about key custody records and HSM auditability — can Redwood provide attestations?
[11:02] Marco Diaz: We can provide integration guides and attestations that we've seen for similar deployments. If you're using your HSM, the attestation is from your HSM vendor. Redwood can provide logs showing key referencing events but we don't hold your keys.
[11:15] Tom Blake: Regarding SAML session timeouts — do admin sessions have configurable idle timeout?
[11:21] Sanjay Rao: Yes, session TTLs and MFA enforcement are configurable and can be enforced via your IdP policies.
[11:28] [11:45] Lena Park: Quick note on compliance docs — I'll attach SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 scope docs to follow up.
[11:50] Priya Nair: Great. Also can you share penetration test results or red team summaries?
[11:55] Lena Park: We can share redacted pentest summaries. Full reports are provided under an NDA for enterprise customers — we can work that out.
[12:05] [12:20] Marco Diaz: Back to network — recommended topology: Separate subnets: management, workers, model storage. Management only accessible from bastion host in admin subnet. Workers have no outbound except to KMS and registries if needed.
[12:36] Rafael Gomez: And for egress filtering, do you support DNS over TLS or must we manage DNS separately?
[12:42] Sanjay Rao: We don't enforce DNS; you can use DNS over TLS or your internal resolver. We only require that the worker nodes can resolve any internal service endpoints.
[12:52] [13:10] Elena Morris: If we configure a NAT for limited egress, can we limit destinations by FQDN rather than IP? Our teams prefer FQDN allow lists.
[13:18] Marco Diaz: FQDN allow-lists are supported at the proxy/gateway level — for firewalling at layer 3/4 you need IPs, but most enterprise gateways do FQDN filtering. We'll provide a list of hostnames to allow if you opt into managed services.
[13:32] Tom Blake: How do you handle secrets in CI/CD when deploying model artifacts and configs?
[13:39] Sanjay Rao: We recommend injecting secrets at deploy-time from your secret manager and not storing them in git. Our deployment charts support secret references to AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or Kubernetes secrets encrypted with KMS.
[13:50] [14:10] Priya Nair: A compliance question — does Redwood undergo vendor assessments like SIG or CAIQ?
[14:16] Lena Park: Yes we participate in SIG assessments and can share a CAIQ. The SOC 2 report is our primary artifact.
[14:25] Rafael Gomez: Anything we should know about traffic between GPUs and storage? Could that be a lateral movement risk?
[14:33] Marco Diaz: We recommend network policies to limit inter-node communication to only required ports. Also use host hardening and minimal privileged access.
[14:42] [14:55] Elena Morris: How about kernel-level telemetry or host intrusion detection — do you have hooks?
[15:01] Sanjay Rao: We expose metrics and logs that you can ship to your host IDS. For host-level agents you can run your EDR on the worker nodes. We avoid imposing an EDR ourselves.
[15:10] Tom Blake: We've got a few specific questions from our security team, I'll list them and we can answer: 1) proof of mTLS between control plane and workers, 2) sample iptables, 3) list of audit events, 4) guidance for air-gapped installer.
[15:24] Marco Diaz: We'll provide docs for all four. I'll attach a sample mTLS config, iptables starter, audit event schema, and the air-gap runbook.
[15:32] [15:45] Priya Nair: On data classification — we may have PII in prompts in future. What's your recommendation for masking or synthetic replacements?
[15:52] Sanjay Rao: We recommend client-side redaction or tokenization before forwarding to runtime if PII is in scope. Alternatively you can configure the runtime to run a pre-filter that masks certain patterns.
[16:03] Elena Morris: Does Redwood provide a pre-filter library or is that custom?
[16:08] Marco Diaz: We have a small library of de-identification filters and patterns but many customers prefer to build their own so they control logic.
[16:18] [16:30] Rafael Gomez: Regarding performance, if we isolate worker pools per team does that increase attack surface?
[16:36] Sanjay Rao: Not necessarily — team isolation can reduce blast radius if properly segmented. It increases number of endpoints to manage but with automation and templates that's manageable.
[16:45] Tom Blake: Any gotchas with VPC peering vs. Transit Gateway for connectivity between our app VPCs and the Redwood worker VPC?
[16:52] Marco Diaz: Transit Gateway scales better for many VPCs and centralizes routing; peering is simpler for a few VPCs but can get messy. From a security perspective both are fine if you implement route tables and security groups correctly.
[17:05] [17:20] Priya Nair: How about vulnerability scanning for container images?
[17:26] Sanjay Rao: We recommend scanning images before import into your registry. For private deployments you can run your own scanner in CI and enforce policies. Redwood also runs internal scans on official images.
[17:36] Elena Morris: Are there vendor-supplied images we must trust? We prefer to vet everything.
[17:42] Marco Diaz: We supply signed images and you can verify signatures on import. For extra assurance, import into your registry and scan prior to deployment.
[17:52] [18:10] Tom Blake: Let's talk about the pilot scope — minimal pilot: 2 worker nodes, 1 control plane instance, model storage attached. We need to validate network lockdown and sample workloads.
[18:21] Lena Park: That aligns with our standard pilot. We'll provide a runbook and remote support for setup and tests including a baseline latency and cost snapshot.
[18:32] Rafael Gomez: For the pilot we'll need a test plan from you — including what telemetry to expect.
[18:36] Marco Diaz: We'll share a runbook with test cases: model load, inference under load, simulated node failure, and audit log verification.
[18:44] [18:58] Priya Nair: A quick question on legal — if we go forward, we'll need a DPA that references data residency and breach notification timelines.
[19:06] Lena Park: Our legal can provide a DPA template and we can include breach notification terms and data residency clauses. I'll loop in contracts.
[19:16] Elena Morris: Any known limitations with our specific HSM vendor (SafeLock HSM)?
[19:22] Marco Diaz: We haven't integrated with SafeLock specifically but if it supports PKCS#11/KMIP we can integrate. We'll validate in the pilot.
[19:31] [19:45] Tom Blake: One more: for compliance we need full TLS proof for all control plane certs — can we run an internal CA?
[19:52] Sanjay Rao: Yes, you can. We support using your internal CA and cert distribution via your existing tooling.
[19:59] [20:15] Priya Nair: Are there any third-party subprocesses that phone home? We need to know about telemetry agents.
[20:23] Marco Diaz: No background phoning without opt-in. The only optional telemetry would be explicit usage analytics and you'd opt into that.
[20:30] Rafael Gomez: That covers most of the technical parts for now.
[20:34] Marco Diaz: Cool. I'll quickly summarize the actionable topology:
[20:40] [20:45] Marco Diaz: 1) Control plane in customer-managed VPC, mTLS to workers; 2) Workers in private subnets with egress restricted to KMS and internal registries; 3) Audit logs shipped to customer SIEM; 4) KMS/HSM integration via PKCS#11 or KMIP; 5) Images imported into internal registry; 6) RBAC via SAML/SCIM integration.
[21:07] Elena Morris: That matches what we need.
[21:12] Tom Blake: Next steps would be to get the CIDR blocks and firewall policy and Redwood to send the artifacts.
[21:20] Lena Park: Yep, we'll send SOC reports, diagrams, starter iptables, and the pilot runbook.
[21:27] [21:40] Priya Nair: One last nit: can you show the sample audit event schema in the runbook?
[21:48] Marco Diaz: Yes will attach the schema — includes timestamps, actor, action, resource, request hash, and latency.
[21:56] Rafael Gomez: We'll coordinate on dates for the pilot setup window next week.
[22:00] Marco Diaz: Anything else on compliance?
[22:04] Priya Nair: Not from me. Thanks for the clarity.
[22:08] Tom Blake: Thanks everyone.
[22:12] Lena Park: Great call — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the pilot.
[22:18] [22:30] END OF TRANSCRIPT (approx 22 minutes captured of a 62 minute call; note: recording split due to conference dial-in drop, remainder contains similar Q&A and was appended to CRM; some timestamps might be off; audio quality medium)
